title: The Meaning of the Millennium: Four Views
summary: The classic evangelical multi-view volume on the millennium (InterVarsity Press). Each of four scholars sets out his position on Revelation 20 and the shape of the end, and the other three respond. It defined the four-way categories most later discussions use.
keyPoints: Ladd argues that Revelation 20 follows the Second Coming of Revelation 19 and that the two resurrections of Revelation 20:4-6 must both be bodily.
Hoyt defends dispensational premillennialism, stressing literal fulfilment of the covenants with national Israel.
Boettner argues that the gospel will Christianize the world through ordinary means before Christ returns.
Hoekema presents amillennialism as inaugurated eschatology: the millennium is the present reign of Christ and departed saints.
The responses show that hermeneutics (how literally to read prophecy and Revelation) drives most disagreements.

title: Three Views on the Millennium and Beyond
summary: Zondervan Counterpoints volume in which a progressive dispensational premillennialist (Blaising), a postmillennialist (Gentry) and an amillennialist (Strimple) each present their case and respond to the others. It is often regarded as the most exegetically detailed of the millennial multi-view books.
keyPoints: Blaising frames premillennialism within a holistic 'new creation' eschatology that includes nations and Israel.
Gentry grounds postmillennialism in the Abrahamic covenant, the Great Commission and the progressive growth parables of Matthew 13.
Strimple argues that the New Testament teaches one return, one resurrection and one judgment, leaving no room for an interim kingdom.
The exchange highlights disagreement over whether Old Testament prophecies of a glorious future are fulfilled before, at or after Christ's return.

title: Four Views on the Book of Revelation
summary: Zondervan Counterpoints volume on how to interpret Revelation: Gentry (preterist), Hamstra (idealist), Pate (progressive dispensationalist) and Thomas (classical dispensationalist). Each essay walks through the structure and key symbols of Revelation.
keyPoints: Gentry argues for a pre-AD 70 date and reads the bulk of Revelation as Christ's judgment on Jerusalem.
Hamstra presents Revelation as a symbolic portrayal of timeless spiritual conflict and victory.
Pate offers an 'already/not yet' reading combining first-century fulfilment with a future consummation.
Thomas defends a consistent futurist reading of Revelation 4–22 under a literal hermeneutic.
The date of Revelation (pre-70 versus c. 95) emerges as a disputed hinge for the preterist case.

title: Revelation: Four Views — A Parallel Commentary
summary: A single-author reference work that sets historicist, preterist, futurist and spiritual (idealist) interpretations of each passage of Revelation in parallel columns, summarizing what representative commentators say without adjudicating. The revised edition expands the sources and adds discussion of full preterism.
keyPoints: Presents each school in the words and logic of its own commentators.
Introduces the date-of-Revelation debate and the major millennial views.
Shows how the same symbol (e.g. the Beast, Babylon, the 144,000) is read differently by each school.
Widely used in churches and classrooms as a neutral starting point.

title: Three Views on the Rapture: Pretribulation, Prewrath, or Posttribulation
summary: Second-edition Counterpoints volume that replaces the midtribulational view with prewrath. Blaising argues for pretribulationism, Hultberg for the prewrath rapture, and Moo for posttribulationism, each with responses.
keyPoints: Blaising grounds pretribulationism in the Day of the Lord coming as a whole, beginning with the tribulation, from which the church is exempt (1 Thessalonians 5:9).
Hultberg argues the church endures the Antichrist's persecution but is rescued before God's wrath at the sixth seal.
Moo argues the parallels between the Olivet Discourse and Paul point to a single posttribulational coming.
All three are futurist premillennialists, so the debate is intramural.

title: The Rapture: Pre-, Mid-, or Post-Tribulational?
summary: Zondervan multi-view book (later reissued as Three Views on the Rapture) in which Feinberg defends pretribulationism, Archer midtribulationism and Moo posttribulationism, with an opening history of the debate by Reiter. A contemporary Bibliotheca Sacra review called it comprehensive, scholarly and irenic.
keyPoints: Reiter traces the rapture debate in American evangelicalism since the Niagara Bible Conferences.
Feinberg argues the church is promised exemption from the wrath that characterizes the whole seventieth week.
Archer places the rapture at the midpoint of Daniel's seventieth week, before the great tribulation.
Moo argues for a single coming after the tribulation from Matthew 24 and 2 Thessalonians 2.

title: The Great Tribulation: Past or Future? Two Evangelicals Debate the Question
summary: Kregel debate book in which Gentry argues that the great tribulation of Matthew 24 was fulfilled in the Jewish War of AD 66-70, and Ice argues that it is a future seven-year period before Christ's return. Each writes opening statements and rebuttals.
keyPoints: Gentry stresses 'this generation' (Matthew 24:34) and the local, Judean focus of the warnings (Matthew 24:16-20).
Ice argues 'this generation' refers to the generation that sees the signs and that the cosmic signs and global scope demand a future fulfilment.
The two disagree over whether Luke 21:20-24 interprets the 'abomination of desolation' as the Roman armies.
Both affirm a future bodily return of Christ and reject full preterism.

title: Covenantal and Dispensational Theologies: Four Views on the Continuity of Scripture
participants: Brent E. Parker and Richard J. Lucas (eds.)
summary: IVP Academic Spectrum volume comparing the four main evangelical frameworks for relating the testaments: covenant theology, progressive covenantalism, progressive dispensationalism and traditional dispensationalism. Each contributor argues and responds.
keyPoints: Horton presents the covenants of redemption, works and grace as the Bible's architecture.
Wellum argues that the biblical covenants progressively reach their fulfilment in Christ and the new covenant.
Bock argues for an inaugurated Davidic kingdom with a future for national Israel.
Snoeberger defends a traditional dispensational distinction between Israel and the church.
Frameworks, not just texts, shape conclusions about Israel, the land and the millennium.

title: Perspectives on Israel and the Church: 4 Views
participants: Chad O. Brand and Tom Pratt Jr.
summary: B&H Academic volume on the relationship of Israel and the church: traditional covenantal (Reymond), traditional dispensational (Thomas), progressive dispensational (Saucy) and progressive covenantal (Brand and Pratt), each with responses.
keyPoints: Reymond sees the church as the continuation and fulfilment of true Israel.
Thomas argues for a strict distinction between Israel and the church under a grammatical-historical hermeneutic.
Saucy allows more continuity while affirming a future for national Israel.
Brand and Pratt read Israel's promises as fulfilled typologically in Christ and his people.

title: Three Views on Israel and the Church: Perspectives on Romans 9–11
participants: Jared Compton and Andrew David Naselli (eds.)
Fred G. Zaspel and James M. Hamilton Jr.
summary: Kregel Academic volume focused on Romans 9–11 and especially the meaning of 'all Israel will be saved' (Romans 11:26).
keyPoints: Vlach argues for a future mass conversion of ethnic Israel and a continuing national role for Israel.
Zaspel and Hamilton expect a future mass conversion but no separate role for Israel apart from the church.
Merkle argues Paul promises the salvation of an elect remnant throughout the age, not a future mass conversion.
The debate cuts across millennial lines: postmillennialists and many amillennialists also differ on Romans 11.

title: Debate on Christian Reconstruction and Dominion Theology (Dallas)
summary: Public debate on 14 April 1988 in Dallas, hosted by Dominion Press, between dispensationalists Dave Hunt and Thomas Ice and Christian Reconstructionists Gary North and Gary DeMar. It focused on postmillennial 'dominion' and the application of biblical law. DeMar's book The Debate Over Christian Reconstruction is his summary and reply.
keyPoints: Ice challenged the exegetical basis of postmillennialism; Hunt criticized the Reconstructionist programme for society.
North and DeMar argued that Christ's present kingship and the Great Commission imply the progressive discipling of nations.
The debate was part of a wider late-1980s literary exchange (House and Ice, DeMar and Leithart, Bahnsen and Gentry).
Accounts come mainly from participants on each side; no neutral report of the outcome was found.

title: Second Dallas debate on Dominion Theology (John Ankerberg Show / NRB)
summary: According to Thomas Ice, a second debate took place in Dallas on 29 July 1989, sponsored by The John Ankerberg Show and the National Religious Broadcasters. Greg Bahnsen was scheduled but withdrew for health reasons, so DeMar joined Gentry for the Reconstructionist side.
keyPoints: Continued the 1988 debate on postmillennialism and theonomy.
Gentry's participation linked the debate to his preterist-postmillennial exegesis.
Details come from Ice's own account; no transcript was located.

title: Preterism vs. Futurism (Biola University)
summary: A recorded debate on 26 February 2002 at Biola University on whether the Olivet Discourse and related prophecies are past or future. It was followed by written exchanges, including DeMar's article 'On Thin Ice' and Ice's reply 'On Solid Ground'.
keyPoints: DeMar argued from the second-person 'you' and 'this generation' that Jesus addressed his own hearers.
Ice countered that the generic 'you' (as in Deuteronomy 4 and 30) can address the nation across generations.
DeMar's critique targeted dispensational timelines, not the hope of a future Second Coming.
Each side later disputed the other's account of what had been answered.

title: The Great Tribulation: Past or Future? (Ice vs. DeMar)
summary: Thomas Ice reports a further debate with Gary DeMar on 26 May 2006 under the title 'The Great Tribulation: Past or Future?', revisiting the questions of his 1999 book with Kenneth Gentry.
keyPoints: Focused on whether Matthew 24:15-31 was fulfilled in AD 70.
Same title and issues as the Ice-Gentry book (1999).
Date and title come from Ice's writings; venue and recording were not confirmed.

title: An Evening of Eschatology
summary: A two-hour moderated roundtable held 27 September 2009 at Bethlehem Baptist Church in Minneapolis, sponsored by Desiring God and Bethlehem College & Seminary. Hamilton (historic premillennial), Storms (amillennial) and Wilson (postmillennial) presented and cross-examined one another; Piper said he holds historic premillennialism and regards amillennialism as the next most plausible view.
keyPoints: Hamilton read Revelation 19–20 sequentially, with the millennium following Christ's return.
Storms read Revelation 20 as the present reign of Christ and departed saints, recapitulating the church age.
Wilson argued that Christ reigns now and the gospel will progressively disciple the nations before his return.
A notably irenic example of all three millennial views debated by Reformed evangelicals together.

title: Dr. Brown Debates Gary DeMar on Israel and the Church
summary: Audio debate hosted by The Line of Fire on 'replacement theology', Israel's role in prophecy and God's future purposes for the Jewish people. Brown, a Messianic Jewish historic premillennialist, defended a distinct future for ethnic Israel; DeMar, a postmillennial partial preterist, argued that the church is the continuation of true Israel while rejecting the 'replacement' label.
keyPoints: Disagreement centred on Romans 11 and the Old Testament restoration promises.
Brown stressed promised national deliverance and the embrace of the Messiah by Israel.
DeMar stressed New Testament fulfilment of Israel's hopes in Christ.
Date and full content were not confirmed.

title: Dr. Brown Debates Don Preston on Romans 11
summary: Line of Fire debate in which full preterist Don Preston argued that the salvation of 'all Israel' in Romans 11 was fulfilled by AD 70, and Brown argued for a still-future national turning of Israel to the Messiah tied to Christ's future return.
keyPoints: Centred on Romans 11:25-27 and its citation of Isaiah 59.
Preston links the 'coming of the Deliverer' to the AD 70 consummation of the old covenant.
Brown affirms a future bodily return and resurrection, which Preston denies.
Date and full content were not confirmed.

title: Dr. Brown Debates Michael Sullivan on Full Preterism
summary: Line of Fire debate in which Sullivan, a 'sovereign grace' full preterist, argued that the Second Coming, resurrection and judgment were fulfilled at the end of the old covenant age in AD 70; Brown defended the historic expectation of a future bodily return and resurrection.
keyPoints: Sullivan builds on New Testament time-statements ('at hand', 'this generation').
Brown appeals to bodily-resurrection texts such as 1 Corinthians 15 and the creedal consensus.
Illustrates how full preterism is engaged by premillennialists as well as by Reformed postmillennialists and amillennialists.
Date and full content were not confirmed.

title: Dominion Theology: Blessing or Curse? and House Divided (print exchange)
summary: A book-length printed debate. House and Ice (Multnomah, 1988) critiqued theonomy and Reconstructionist postmillennialism from a dispensational perspective; Bahnsen and Gentry replied point by point in House Divided: The Break-Up of Dispensational Theology (1989), defending theonomic postmillennialism and criticizing dispensationalism.
keyPoints: House and Ice argued that the Mosaic law does not bind the nations today and that the church age ends in apostasy, not triumph.
Bahnsen defended the continuing validity of God's law; Gentry defended postmillennial exegesis.
Ice had himself been a theonomist until 1986, which lent the exchange intensity.
Each side regarded the other's book as a decisive answer.

title: The Apocalypse Code and Breaking the Apocalypse Code (print exchange)
summary: Hanegraaff's The Apocalypse Code (2007) attacked the Left Behind style of dispensational futurism and proposed an 'exegetical eschatology' reading much of Revelation as fulfilled in AD 70. Ice reviewed it critically and, with Mark Hitchcock, published Breaking the Apocalypse Code in reply.
keyPoints: Hanegraaff argued for an early date of Revelation and against Christian Zionism.
Ice and Hitchcock argued that Hanegraaff misrepresented Tim LaHaye and abandoned a literal hermeneutic.
Both sides affirm a future bodily return and resurrection.
Publisher and year of the Ice-Hitchcock book were not confirmed online.

title: When Shall These Things Be? A Reformed Response to Hyper-Preterism
summary: A multi-author Reformed critique of full ('hyper') preterism by amillennial and postmillennial scholars, addressing creeds, history, hermeneutics, the resurrection and the Second Coming. Full preterists published replies arguing that the critics did not answer the time-texts.
keyPoints: Argues that the creeds' affirmation of future return and resurrection reflects the church's universal reading of Scripture.
Several chapters examine the resurrection texts (1 Corinthians 15) and argue they require a future bodily resurrection.
Gentry argues that partial preterists can consistently distinguish AD 70 from the final coming.
Notable as postmillennialists and amillennialists jointly opposing full preterism.

title: He Shall Have Dominion: A Postmillennial Eschatology
summary: Widely regarded as the most comprehensive modern defense of postmillennialism, combining biblical theology of the covenants, exegesis of Old Testament kingdom prophecies and the Great Commission, and a preterist reading of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation.
keyPoints: Traces a theme of redemptive victory from Genesis 3:15 through the Abrahamic and Davidic covenants.
Reads Psalm 110 and 1 Corinthians 15:24-26 as Christ reigning until his enemies are subdued before his return.
Argues the kingdom grows gradually like leaven and mustard seed (Matthew 13).
Answers objections drawn from texts on apostasy and suffering.

title: Before Jerusalem Fell: Dating the Book of Revelation
summary: A detailed argument for a Neronic date of Revelation (c. AD 65–66), examining external evidence (including the interpretation of Irenaeus) and internal evidence (the temple in Revelation 11, the seven kings of Revelation 17). The date is disputed; late-date scholars such as Beale and Hitchcock reply that the external evidence for c. AD 95 is strong.
keyPoints: Argues Irenaeus's statement may refer to John, not the vision, being seen under Domitian (a disputed reading).
Reads Revelation 11:1-2 as presupposing the temple still standing.
Identifies the sixth king of Revelation 17:10 with Nero.
Links 666 to the gematria of 'Nero Caesar' in Hebrew letters.

title: A Case for Amillennialism: Understanding the End Times
summary: An accessible defense of amillennialism as the historic Protestant view, organized around the 'two-age' structure of New Testament eschatology and Christ's present reign.
keyPoints: Argues that 'this age' and 'the age to come' leave no room for an interim millennium.
Reads Revelation 20 as recapitulating the church age.
Critiques dispensational and postmillennial readings of Daniel 9 and Romans 11.
Explains the 'already/not yet' as tension between present victory and present suffering.

title: Kingdom Come: The Amillennial Alternative
summary: A thorough exegetical defense of amillennialism by a former dispensationalist, covering Daniel's seventy weeks, the Olivet Discourse, Romans 11, 2 Thessalonians 2 and Revelation 20, with chapters interacting with premillennialism and postmillennialism.
keyPoints: Argues that 1 Corinthians 15:23-26 places the defeat of death at Christ's return, ruling out post-return death in a millennium.
Reads Revelation 20:1-3 as Satan restrained from deceiving the nations during the gospel age.
Accepts preterist readings of much of the Olivet Discourse.
Critiques postmillennialism for underweighting suffering in the present age.

title: The Bible and the Future
summary: A standard Reformed textbook on eschatology covering both personal and cosmic eschatology, notable for 'inaugurated eschatology' and its emphasis on the new earth.
keyPoints: Argues that the New Testament presents the end as already begun in Christ.
Argues the final hope is a renewed earth, not an ethereal heaven.
Prefers 'realized millennialism' as a positive label for amillennialism.
Includes critiques of dispensational premillennialism.

title: A Case for Historic Premillennialism: An Alternative to 'Left Behind' Eschatology
participants: Craig L. Blomberg and Sung Wook Chung (eds.)
summary: A multi-author case for premillennialism without dispensational distinctives and with a posttribulational rapture, drawing on church history, the Old Testament, the Gospels, Paul and Revelation.
keyPoints: Argues the early church's chiliasm was historic premillennial, not dispensational.
Reads Revelation 19–20 sequentially, with two bodily resurrections.
Rejects a pretribulational rapture in favour of a single return.
Presents the view as a middle way between dispensationalism and amillennialism.

title: Things to Come: A Study in Biblical Eschatology
summary: The classic comprehensive textbook of classical dispensational eschatology, covering hermeneutics, the biblical covenants, the rapture, Daniel's seventieth week, the millennium and the eternal state.
keyPoints: Argues for a consistent literal hermeneutic as the basis of premillennialism.
Treats the Abrahamic, Davidic and New covenants as unconditional promises to national Israel.
Defends a pretribulational rapture.
Describes the millennium as the fulfilment of Israel's kingdom promises.

title: Progressive Dispensationalism
summary: The defining statement of progressive dispensationalism, which sees the dispensations as progressive stages in one plan and the Davidic kingdom as already inaugurated, while retaining a future for Israel and a premillennial return.
keyPoints: Argues Christ now reigns on David's throne at the Father's right hand (Acts 2:30-36).
Sees the church as a stage in, not a parenthesis to, the kingdom programme.
Maintains a future national and territorial restoration of Israel.
Moves toward a holistic new-creation eschatology.

title: Kingdom through Covenant: A Biblical-Theological Understanding of the Covenants
summary: A major biblical-theological study of the covenants proposing 'progressive covenantalism' as a middle way between covenant theology and dispensationalism.
keyPoints: Traces the covenants from creation to the new covenant as the backbone of the biblical story.
Argues typology escalates to fulfilment in Christ.
Reads Israel's land promise as fulfilled in the new creation.
Rejects both a single covenant of grace and a separate future plan for national Israel.

title: The Parousia
summary: A systematic study of every New Testament reference to Christ's coming, concluding that all were fulfilled within the apostolic generation, culminating in AD 70. It is the founding classic of full preterism and is also cited by partial preterists for its time-text analysis. Critics note that its conclusions deny the creedal future bodily resurrection and return.
keyPoints: Treats the time-statements ('soon', 'at hand', 'this generation') as decisive.
Reads the Olivet Discourse, Thessalonians and Revelation as one prophetic horizon.
Applies the resurrection and judgment to the AD 70 transition.
Remains in print and influential among full and partial preterists.

title: The Puritan Hope: Revival and the Interpretation of Prophecy
summary: A historical study of the eschatological hope of the English and Scottish Puritans and their heirs, centred on the future conversion of the Jews (Romans 11) and the worldwide spread of the gospel, and its role in the modern missionary movement.
keyPoints: Traces the hope through Owen, the Westminster divines, Edwards and the early missionaries.
Highlights Romans 11 as the key text for a future large-scale conversion of Israel.
Connects eschatology with prayer for revival.
Often credited with reviving historic postmillennialism among Reformed evangelicals.

title: The City of God, Book XX
summary: Augustine's treatment of the last judgment, including his influential reading of Revelation 20 as the present age of the church, which dominated Western interpretation for a millennium.
keyPoints: The binding of Satan is his restraint from seducing the nations, allowing the church's growth.
The first resurrection is spiritual regeneration; the second is bodily.
The thousand years signifies the whole period of the church (or a perfect number).
Augustine notes he once held a form of chiliasm before rejecting carnal versions of it.

title: The Book of Revelation (New International Greek Testament Commentary)
summary: A massive exegetical commentary arguing for a 'redemptive-historical form of modified idealism' and a late (c. AD 95) date, with extensive attention to Old Testament allusions.
keyPoints: Revelation's visions recapitulate the age between Christ's comings.
Old Testament allusions (especially Daniel) are the key to the symbols.
Revelation 20 depicts the present reign of believers and Satan's restraint.
Defends the late date while acknowledging the strength of some early-date arguments.

title: Not Afraid of the Antichrist: Why We Don't Believe in a Pre-Tribulation Rapture
summary: Two charismatic scholars argue from the New Testament that believers will face the end-time tribulation and that Christ's return is a single posttribulational event.
keyPoints: Argues the rapture and the Second Coming are the same event (Matthew 24:29-31; 1 Thessalonians 4).
Holds that 'wrath' from which believers are spared is God's judgment, not persecution.
Encourages readiness for suffering rather than escape.
Pretribulational reviewers argue the authors misread the Day of the Lord texts.

title: The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church
summary: The book that popularized the prewrath view, placing the rapture after the great tribulation begins but before the Day of the Lord's wrath, within the second half of Daniel's seventieth week.
keyPoints: Distinguishes the 'great tribulation' (man's and Satan's wrath) from the Day of the Lord (God's wrath).
Links the cosmic signs of the sixth seal (Revelation 6:12-17) with Matthew 24:29.
Argues the church sees the Antichrist (2 Thessalonians 2:1-4).
Critiqued by pretribulationists for dividing the seventieth week.

title: Horae Apocalypticae
summary: The most elaborate historicist commentary on Revelation, correlating each seal, trumpet and vial with events in church history using the day-year principle.
keyPoints: Reads the trumpets as barbarian and Islamic invasions of the Roman world.
Identifies the papacy as the Beast and Antichrist.
Uses the day-year principle for the 1,260 days.
Shows both the learning and the difficulty of fixing prophetic dates.

title: The Last Days According to Jesus
summary: A popular-level defense of partial preterism that takes the time-texts of the Olivet Discourse seriously in reply to skeptics, while affirming a future return and rejecting full preterism.
keyPoints: Uses Bertrand Russell's objection to Jesus' predictions as a starting point.
Reads 'this generation' as Jesus' contemporaries.
Distinguishes partial from full preterism.
Engages Gentry's case for an early date of Revelation.

title: Jesus and the Victory of God
summary: A major historical study of Jesus that reads the Olivet Discourse's 'coming of the Son of Man' as Jesus' vindication and the judgment on Jerusalem, interpreted through Daniel 7 and Jewish apocalyptic imagery.
keyPoints: Apocalyptic cosmic language describes socio-political events with theological significance.
Jesus predicted the temple's fall as divine judgment.
The 'coming' of Daniel 7 is upward to God, signifying vindication.
Wright still affirms a future bodily resurrection and new creation.
